metric.why: A facility can have enough total cooling and still starve individual racks; airflow and pressure sensors find recirculation, bypass, and leaks that temperature averages hide.
metric.definition: Cubic feet per minute delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it through equipment rather than around it.

reading.body:
Aggregate cooling capacity in a data center can be fully adequate while individual racks overheat, and airflow and static pressure measurement is the tool that reveals that gap.

Total cooling figures, whether reported in tons of refrigeration or kilowatts of heat rejection, describe the room as a whole. Airflow measured in cubic feet per minute, combined with the pressure differential that forces air through equipment rather than around it, shows whether conditioned air reaches specific racks or bleeds away through recirculation, bypass paths, or physical leaks. For AI workloads this distinction is acute, because GPU and accelerator racks run at power densities that punish uneven distribution, and a single rack starved of airflow can throttle or fail regardless of what the room-level average shows.

The data covers one operational metric within the broader cooling and climate category. It sits alongside temperature and humidity monitoring and liquid coolant tracking, which together form the instrumentation layer for cooling oversight. What this metric does not address is power draw, water consumption, or the facility-level constraints that set the ceiling on how much heat any cooling system can remove in the first place. It is a diagnostic tool for distribution, not a measure of total capacity or of the grid demand that capacity creates.
